title: The Ungrateful Man (தமிழ்)
summary: In a quiet village near the Vindhya hills lived an impoverished, kind-hearted Brahmin named Yajnadatta. Traveling through the wilderness ... [TA]
full_text:
In a quiet village near the Vindhya hills lived an impoverished, kind-hearted Brahmin named Yajnadatta. Traveling through the wilderness in search of employment, he came upon a deep, abandoned well whose masonry had collapsed. Hearing pitiful cries rising from the dark pit, the Brahmin leaned over the stone rim and peered down.

Trapped at the muddy bottom were four miserable creatures: a fierce tiger, an ape, a venomous black cobra, and a man dressed in fine merchant's robes.

Seeing the holy man, the tiger pleaded: 'O compassionate Brahmin, throw down a rope and rescue me! I swear by the sacred mountains that I will never harm you, but will repay your kindness!'

Yajnadatta hesitated, fearing the predator's claws, but pity moved his heart. Lowering a strong vine rope, he hauled the heavy tiger to safety. The tiger bowed low and said: 'I dwell in the cavern of the southern ridge. If you ever pass that way and need food, visit my cave.'

The Brahmin lowered the vine again and pulled up the ape. The ape chattered gratefully: 'I live in the wild mango grove on the cliff. Whenever you hunger, come, and I will shake down sweet fruits for you.'

Next, the black cobra called from the mud: 'Rescue me also, O gentle sage! Though my bite is death to the wicked, I will never harm my savior. If ever you find yourself in mortal danger, remember me, and I will come to your aid.' The Brahmin pulled up the serpent, who thanked him and slithered into the grass.

As the Brahmin prepared to depart, the four creatures warned him in unison: 'Revered master, leave the fourth prisoner in the pit! Do not rescue that man. Humans are deceitful, treacherous, and ungrateful; if you save him, he will repay your kindness with ruin.'

Yet the tender-hearted Brahmin thought: 'He is a fellow human being; how can I leave him to starve in a dark hole?' He lowered the vine a fourth time and hauled the man out of the well.

The rescued man prostrated himself, saying: 'I am Suvarnakara, a master goldsmith in the capital city of Ujjayini. If you ever visit the city and have gold or silver to work, come to my shop, and I will serve you with all my skill.'

Months passed, and extreme poverty struck the Brahmin's household. Remembering the promises, Yajnadatta journeyed into the forest. He visited the ape, who joyfully filled his basket with delicious wild mangoes, figs, and honey. He then visited the tiger's cave; the noble beast welcomed him, bowed his head, and laid at his feet a magnificent golden necklace and jeweled ornaments (which the tiger had taken from a prince who had fallen from his horse in the forest).

Delighted, the Brahmin thought: 'These ornaments will banish my poverty forever! I will take them to the goldsmith whom I rescued; he will melt them down honestly and pay me their true value in silver.'

Entering the goldsmith's shop in Ujjayini, Yajnadatta presented the jewels. The greedy artisan immediately recognized the necklace: it belonged to the King's son, who had recently disappeared in the forest!

Instead of gratitude, dark ambition seized the goldsmith: 'If I surrender this beggar to the King as the prince's murderer, the King will reward me with immense riches and royal favor!'

Ordering the Brahmin to rest while he evaluated the gold, the treacherous goldsmith ran straight to the royal palace and informed the King that the prince's assassin was in his shop. Royal guards seized the bewildered Brahmin, bound him in heavy chains, and cast him into the deepest dungeon, sentenced to be impaled upon the stake at dawn.

Sitting in the cold, rat-infested cell, the weeping Brahmin remembered the warning of the beasts: 'Alas! The tiger, the ape, and the cobra spoke the truth. The human alone was devoid of honor.'

Remembering the cobra's promise, he called the serpent in his heart. Instantly, the black cobra slipped through the dungeon bars and coiled at his feet: 'What is your command, my savior?'

The Brahmin recounted the goldsmith's betrayal. The cobra said: 'I will avenge you tonight. I will enter the palace bedchamber and bite the King's beloved daughter, the Princess. My venom will resist all physicians, charms, and herbs. No medicine in creation can cure her except the touch of your hand upon her forehead. When the King proclaims that anyone who cures the princess will receive half the kingdom, step forward, touch her brow, and reveal the truth.'

That night, the princess was bitten. The court physicians, sorcerers, and snake-charmers were helpless; the maiden lay cold and breathless on her couch. Proclamations were shouted through the city promising wealth and honors to whoever could neutralize the venom.

The Brahmin informed the dungeon warden that he could cure the princess. Led to the royal bedchamber, Yajnadatta placed his hand upon the maiden's forehead. At his touch, the miraculous venom dissolved; color returned to her cheeks, and she opened her eyes in perfect health!

Overjoyed, the King embraced the Brahmin and asked how he possessed such power. Yajnadatta revealed the entire history—the deep well, the gratitude of the tiger, ape, and snake, the betrayal of the goldsmith, and the true source of the prince's necklace.

The King's wrath fell upon the treacherous artisan. He ordered the ungrateful goldsmith impaled upon the stake, while Yajnadatta was granted a thousand fertile villages, high ministerial office, and lived in honor, proving forever:
"Wild beasts of fang and claw remember kindness well,
And return loyalty from the forest where they dwell;
But the false heart of man turns venomous and cold,
And sells his savior's life for petty crumbs of gold."
moral: Wild beasts remember kindness and return loyalty; but a deceitful, ungrateful human knows no honor. [TA]

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Ungrateful Man"?
options: True wealth lies in contentment and honesty; greed leads to ruin.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.

author: Pandit Vishnu Sharma (~200 BCE – 300 CE)
content_notes: Family-safe traditional adaptation from the Panchatantra anthology. (Localized for Tamil readers, safe for schools and family bedtime).

vocabulary.meaning: wise advice given to guide decisions
the ability to judge well and understand the truth
the ability to remain calm and think clearly during sudden events

discussion_questions.prompt: What is the main situation at the beginning of "The Ungrateful Man"?
Why does this story teach that "True wealth lies in contentment and honesty; greed leads to ruin."?
How could you use this lesson in your own school or family life?
Was the character’s final decision fair and kind to everyone?
Imagine an alternate peaceful ending or a new creative adventure for these characters.

reflection_prompt: Have you ever had to choose between acting quickly in anger or waiting patiently to understand the truth?
activity: Draw a colorful picture of your favorite moment in this story or share the moral with your family.
